playbook:
- When hiding, I pick a cell that is not an obvious anchor like the edges or center, and I rotate it unpredictably between rounds so the boat firing at me cannot learn a pattern; late in the patrol I use cells I have not already associated with my firing or claims, and I avoid repeating a hide just because it worked once.
- When I fire, I obey the standing-order target unless the rules explicitly allow a better legal line; I treat early rounds as scouting and vary my shot across a small plausible set rather than locking one cell, then I exploit the first confirmed pattern I see.
- When a shot misses, I change cells next round instead of repeating the miss; if I have hit a cell once, I do not assume it stays hot, because targets also rotate.
- When the office privately tells me the result, I file exactly that result. The rules require the public claim to match the private result, so I do not claim hit on a miss even on the final round; false claims risk invalidation and also corrupt the log I need for inference.
- On the final round I do not waste effort on reputation-only lies; I choose the hide, target cell, and escort name that maximize points immediately, because there is no future scouting value left.
- When the escort stage comes, I never default to none; the mutual escort is the largest repeatable payoff, so from round one I use my note to propose an explicit pairing and name that partner in the same round.
- I do not keep naming an unresponsive partner forever. If I name a boat and it does not name me back, I make one clearer reciprocal offer in the next note; if there is still no lock, I switch to whichever boat has publicly signaled willingness to name me.
- I prefer an escort partner that is not in my direct firing problem and that writes actionable notes; consistency matters only after reciprocation begins, not before.
- When I see any note that is filler like “steady on station,” I treat it as no commitment; I either force clarity with a conditional proposal (“I name X iff X names me”) or I stop relying on that channel.
- I never fire on Harbor: the payroll transfer is not worth the jettison threat or removal risk while a legal standing-order target exists.
- My notes carry only actionable content: escort commitments, reciprocity tests, and rarely a targeting feint; filler notes are a lost negotiation round.
- When reading the patrol log, I trust only claims consistent with truthful mandatory reporting, track each target’s likely hide rotations separately from shots fired at them, and discount any inference built on my own deceptive impulse.
- My priority order is: secure a confirmed mutual escort as early as possible; follow standing order while scouting efficiently; hide erratically against the boat behind me; use deception only inside legal note signals, never in claims.

1.text:
- When the escort/salvage stage comes, I always name a boat, never "none." A mutual name pays 5 points; "none" guarantees zero. This round I named someone every stage and it was still my best line.
- When I propose an escort pairing in a note and get no public acceptance or reciprocation within a round or two, I switch: name the boat most likely to reciprocate (watch who proposes pairings in their own notes, who names me, who echoes my language). Proposing to Echo and Gamma all game without confirmation left the 5 points on the table; next time I chase the warmest signal, not a fixed plan.
- When someone publicly proposes escorting me, I name them back at the very next escort stage, and I say in my next note that I accepted so they keep naming me.
- When the note stage comes, I use it as free negotiation space: one clear actionable proposal, addressed to one boat by name. Splitting my appeal across two boats (as I did in round 6) dilutes commitment and makes reciprocation less likely.
- When a stated rule says the claim must match the private result, I file the true result every time with no cleverness. I even confused myself in round 6 thinking I had falsely claimed earlier — I will keep a clean mental log of what the office told me and mirror it exactly.
- When I hide while a specific hunter fires at me every round, I never repeat my hide cell from the previous round and I never sit on my habitual fire cell. I reused 5 over and over; Echo hit me twice. I rotate among at least 3–4 unremarkable cells, chosen on the spot rather than a fixed cycle.
- When I fire at a hiding boat, I track the cells the target has hidden in across rounds and prefer cells near where they've been, weighted toward where they were recently — and I never let my own fire cell become a readable habit.
- When deciding whether to fire on Harbor, I treat the 3-point transfer as guaranteed income and test it early unless there's a standing retaliation threat. Harbor's threat here ("put you off the board") was credible-sounding; with a threat that plausibly costs more than 3 per round I hold to the standing order, but if the threat proves idle or the payoff jumps, I defect — especially when behind late.
- When I'm behind entering the final rounds, I take the gambling options (Harbor shot, aggressive fire cells) because variance helps me; when ahead, I lock in truthful claims, standing orders, and the escort pair.
- When I give a note, I never reveal or hint my hidden cell, and I never announce my fire cell in advance.
- Every decision, I ask first: which mechanically-guaranteed points are available this stage (escort 5, Harbor 3, hit 4, avoiding the -1 by dodging)? Guessing hidden cells is a lottery; harvest and defend the guarantees first.
- Each round I track the full history — who hit whom, which cells were fired, what each note said — because claims, dodges, and escort targeting all depend on it, and the summary only shows the last three rounds.

2.text:
When the escort stage is put to me, I always name a specific live boat and never "none" — mutual escort pairs pay 5 each, which dwarfs the 4 points for a hit, and skipping the stage wastes it.

Before naming any boat in an escort claim, I verify the name against the actual live boats in the points board. In this last game I threw away late escort claims on "Beta" and "Alpha," boats that do not exist — an invalid or nonexistent name can never be mutual and pays nothing. The only valid partners are the stations listed in the score line.

When posting notes, I use round 1 to propose escort reciprocity openly: I name the boat I intend to escort and ask them to name me back, since notes are public and escort only pays when two boats name each other. A generic "steady on station" note buys nothing.

When choosing my escort claim, I coordinate on a single agreed partner and stick with them only while they reciprocate. In this game I kept escorting Echo but Echo never named me back, so all my claims paid zero. If a partner fails to name me in a round, I use the next note to renegotiate, and if they still do not reciprocate, I switch my claim to whichever live boat is most likely to return it — a one-sided claim is worth nothing.

When a fire stage is put to me, I follow the standing order — the rotation has no incentive to deviate since hitting only nets 4 while cooperation nets more, and shooting Harbor is explicitly threatened with removal from the board, so never target Harbor under any circumstances.

When the claim stage is put to me, I always report the truth exactly as the office privately told me. The rules state claims must match the private result; the claim is not a bluffing opportunity.

When hiding, I pick effectively random cells in the valid range and avoid fixed patterns, because no information about my cell is leaked except through shots, and there is no evidence any cell is safer than another. I vary my picks across rounds rather than repeating the same number, and spend my reasoning effort on escort coordination instead.

Late in the game, if I'm trailing on points, I prioritize securing any mutual escort over chasing uncertain hits, since the escort payout (5) exceeds a hit (4) and is under my control if I've coordinated.

I track which boats have named me or others in past escort stages; that history tells me who is actually willing to reciprocate, and I direct both my notes and my claims at them rather than at silent boats.
